I farm in Quzhou County on the North China Plain, so at the start of the growing season I would keep to the pattern I trust most: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. That fits my climate, my water situation, my labor ability, and the way I manage risk. I would not scatter my land into many small crops, because I know grain best, it is easier for me to manage through the whole year, and I can sell it reliably. Winter wheat gives me one harvest in early summer, then I can use the same fields for summer maize and get the second harvest in autumn. That two-crop system makes the best use of my land and the local growing season.

I would use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed because I want stable emergence, stronger disease resistance, and better yield than old saved seed. For tillage, I would plough before wheat where the soil is tight and crop straw needs to be mixed in, then use rotary tillage before maize after wheat harvest because time is short and I need to sow fast. I would put most fertilizer into wheat and maize because those are the crops I depend on for income. I would watch water carefully: wheat needs more irrigation here, especially around overwintering recovery, jointing, and grain filling, while maize usually needs fewer irrigations unless summer rain is poor. I would spray only as much as needed to control the usual weeds, aphids, and fungal problems in wheat and the borers and leaf diseases in maize. My goal would be steady yield with costs I can carry, not chasing the highest yield with the highest spending.
